passage:
Dear Trisha,

You asked if I'm still "the temple girl". I am. I still light the lamp every morning, and on Saturdays I cook in the temple kitchen. It steadies me like nothing else.

But something happened at work that I want to tell you. A colleague invited me to a meditation circle. The first few evenings were lovely. Then the leader said that true seekers don't ask questions, and that I should give him a month's salary as proof of surrender.

I felt my stomach tighten. My faith has always had room for questions; Amma taught me to ask the priest "why" when I was six. So I thanked them and stopped going. I asked my colleague to be careful too.

I haven't lost anything. My lamp, my Saturdays, my prayers are still mine. I just keep my eyes open now.

With love,
Lakshmi

qa.a: On Saturdays Lakshmi cooks in the temple kitchen.

qa.a: Lakshmi felt uneasy and alarmed; her stomach tightened at the demand for money and the ban on questions.

qa.a: Lakshmi kept her own prayers and service but left the group once it demanded blind obedience and money, and warned the colleague too.

qa.q: How might the colleague who invited Lakshmi see her decision?
qa.a: The colleague might feel surprised or a little hurt at first, but may also start to notice the warning signs Lakshmi pointed out.

grounding: Shows a young woman keeping her faith, ritual and service while staying wary of a group that demands blind obedience and money.

You want to know how faith and questions fit together for me? I'm Maria, and I learnt that the hard way.

I go to Mass every Sunday in Margao, and I volunteer at the shelter on Wednesdays. That part of my life has never wavered.

Two years ago I joined a healing prayer group at a friend's house. At first it felt warm. Then the leader said doubting him was a sin, and asked each of us to sign over our savings "to the mission."

I couldn't sleep that night. So I went to talk to the old parish priest, who has known me since I was a baby. He listened and said, "God doesn't need you to stop thinking. Faith that forbids questions isn't asking for faith."

I left the group. I still pray, still go to the shelter. And when something asks for my obedience and my money together, I slow down and ask.

qa.q: On which day does Maria volunteer at the shelter?
qa.a: Maria volunteers at the shelter on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling on the night after the leader's request?
qa.a: Maria felt troubled and anxious, unable to sleep after being asked to hand over savings and stop doubting.

qa.q: What wise steps did Maria take?
qa.a: Maria talked to a trusted priest, left the group, and kept Maria's own worship and service while staying wary of demands for obedience and money.

qa.q: How does the old parish priest see the prayer group's demands?
qa.a: The priest sees them as a warning sign, saying faith that forbids questions isn't truly asking for faith.

grounding: Shows a young adult combining faith, ritual and service with critical thinking, leaving a group that demands obedience and money.

passage:
Dear Payal,

Toronto was lonely for the first two months. Work, microwave dinners, video calls with Mummy at odd hours. You know how I get.

Then, one Sunday, I walked into the gurdwara near my flat. An uncle handed me a head covering and pointed me to the langar hall. By evening I was rolling rotis with five aunties who laughed at my lopsided rotis and fed me twice. Now I do seva every weekend. It feels like home.

Last month I brought my colleague Mei, who had never been inside a gurdwara. Some people stared, but one aunty sat her down and explained everything, patiently. Mei came back the next week on her own.

That's what I love most. The door is open, and the food is for anyone who walks in.

Come visit and I'll put you to work in the kitchen.

Baljeet

qa.a: The uncle handed Baljeet a head covering.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel in Toronto before finding the gurdwara?
qa.a: Baljeet felt lonely, with only work, microwave dinners and video calls.

qa.a: It gives Baljeet meaning and support through seva, while staying open and welcoming to outsiders like Mei.

qa.q: How might Mei have felt on her first visit?
qa.a: Mei might have felt nervous when some people stared, then welcomed and at ease when an aunty explained everything, enough to return alone.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding meaning and belonging in a faith community while it stays open to people outside it.

So the podcast wants the story of the Ganpati pandal? Okay. I'm Indu, I'm on the committee in our Nagpur colony, and this happened last year.

The committee is like family. Ten days of aarti, cooking together, kids running around. When my father was in hospital, these people brought food for a month. That's what belonging feels like.

Last year Tejas, who's just moved in and says he doesn't believe in God, offered to help with the lights. One member said, "Only people who do the pooja should be on the committee."

I stood up in the meeting, heart racing. "The pandal is for the whole colony. Tejas can do the lights, and he doesn't have to pray. Everyone eats the prasad."

People argued a bit. Then they said yes. Tejas stayed up till two wiring the lights, and on the last night he danced at the visarjan with everyone.

qa.a: Tejas offered to help with the lights.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when standing up in the meeting?
qa.a: Indu felt nervous, with a racing heart, but also determined to keep the pandal open to everyone.

qa.q: How did Indu balance belonging with openness?
qa.a: Indu valued the committee's support like family, while arguing that people outside the faith could also join and help.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when he heard the member's comment?
qa.a: Tejas might have felt unwelcome and unsure whether to stay, before being included and joining the celebration.

grounding: Shows a young adult who finds meaning in a faith community and speaks up to keep it open to someone outside it.

passage:
Tuesday night.

I'm still shaking. Today I saw the safety officer at the Thane site sign off twenty harness inspections without touching a single harness. Twenty. Men climb on those every day.

My first thought was to shout at him in front of everyone. My second was to post the photos online. I did neither.

Instead I took dated photos of the harnesses and the signed forms. At lunch I told Lalit, who works the night shift. He said, "Mohit, I've seen the same thing. I'll sign with you." Then we found the company's safety complaint address and wrote a plain, factual report with the photos.

Lalit warned me they might move me off the project. He might be right. I'm scared about that.

But I'd rather be moved than read about a fall I could have stopped. Sent the report at 9:14 p.m. Now I'm going to try and sleep.

qa.q: How many harness inspections did the safety officer sign off without checking?
qa.a: The safety officer signed off twenty harness inspections.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling about the report and the risk of being moved?
qa.a: Mohit felt outraged and shaken by the unsafe sign-offs, and scared about being moved off the project, yet determined.

qa.q: How did Mohit channel the anger usefully?
qa.a: Mohit gathered dated evidence, found an ally in Lalit and used the company's proper complaint channel instead of shouting or posting online.

qa.q: How might the workers who climb on those harnesses see Mohit's report if they knew?
qa.a: The workers would probably feel protected and grateful, since the report could prevent a fall.

grounding: Shows a young worker channelling moral outrage at an unsafe institution into evidence, allies and proper channels, accepting personal cost.

"Dhruv! Oh my God. It's been, what, a year?"

"More. I saw your post about the baby. Congratulations."

Vinita and I shared a hostel room for three years. We knew each other's tea orders, exam panics and bad jokes. When she moved to Calgary, we promised to call every week.

For a while we did. Then it was every month. Now it's mostly hearts on each other's photos. I'm Aparna, and for a long time I was hurt about it, as if she'd chosen to leave me behind.

Last month, on her birthday, I sent one long voice note: that I missed her, that I hoped the snow wasn't too bad, and that she didn't need to reply at length.

She replied two days later, three sentences and a photo of her new dog. It stung for an evening.

Then I realised it wasn't nothing. She'd still thought of me. We're different people in different time zones. I kept the photo, made two cups of tea out of habit, and drank both.

qa.q: Where did Vinita move?
qa.a: Vinita moved to Calgary.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when Vinita's reply came two days later?
qa.a: Aparna felt a sting of hurt and disappointment for an evening, then a gentler acceptance.

qa.q: Why was Aparna's single voice note a good way to reach out?
qa.a: It was warm and honest but put no pressure on Vinita to reply at length, leaving room for the friendship's new shape.

qa.q: How might Vinita see the change in their friendship?
qa.a: Vinita may still care but be busy with a new life, a new dog and a different time zone, so short replies may feel natural to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult reaching out once to a drifting friend without pressure and accepting the natural change in closeness.

I was waiting for the same Pune bus as Yogesh, a man I'd seen at the stand a few times, when a young woman came up to him crying. She said her bag had been stolen and she needed money for a ticket to Satara.

I couldn't tell what Yogesh was thinking. He looked at her for a moment, clearly sorry for her. Then he said, "I won't give cash, but I'll buy your ticket at the counter myself."

She hesitated. "Just give me the money, it's faster."

He shook his head and pointed to the police booth ten metres away. "They can help you report the bag too. I'll walk over with you."

She suddenly said she'd call her brother instead, and walked off quickly.

Yogesh let out a breath and got on the bus. He looked uncomfortable, and I heard him mutter, "I hope she really gets home."

qa.q: Where did the woman say she needed a ticket to?
qa.a: She said she needed a ticket to Satara.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when the woman walked off quickly?
qa.a: Yogesh felt uncomfortable and uncertain, relieved not to be tricked but still worried that she might really need help.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's response both kind and careful?
qa.a: He offered to buy the ticket directly and walk her to the police booth, helping within safe limits instead of giving cash under pressure.

qa.q: How might the observer see Yogesh's choice?
qa.a: The observer seems to respect it, noticing both his sympathy and his caution without knowing exactly what he thought.

grounding: Shows a young man helping a stranger within safe limits, checking the story and not giving in to pressure.

Monday. A man in a torn shirt stopped Chetan outside his Kolkata office. "I'm Arnab. I lost my job, my child is sick, please help." Chetan felt a pang, and bought him a meal from the stall nearby. Arnab thanked him warmly.

Thursday. Arnab was back. This time the story was different: his wife was in hospital and he needed two thousand rupees today. Chetan felt the pull of guilt, and also a small alarm. The story didn't match.

"I can't give cash," Chetan said gently. "But I'll buy you lunch again, and there's a free shelter on Park Street. I'll write the address."

Arnab's face hardened. "You people never really help," he said, and walked off.

A week later. Chetan still thought about it sometimes, uneasy. He'd started giving a little each month to a shelter that checks who needs help, and he kept a few of their address cards in his wallet.

qa.q: What did Chetan buy Arnab on Monday?
qa.a: Chetan bought him a meal from the stall nearby.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on Thursday when Arnab asked for money?
qa.a: Chetan felt guilty and pulled to help, but also alarmed because the story had changed.

qa.q: How did Chetan stay compassionate but safe?
qa.a: He offered food and the shelter's address instead of cash, didn't give in to the guilt, and later supported a shelter that checks needs.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when Chetan refused cash?
qa.a: Arnab seemed frustrated and angry, saying people never really help, though his full situation remains unclear.

grounding: Shows a young man helping a stranger within safe limits, noticing a changing story and not giving in to guilt or pressure.

Soo-ah posted her new ceramics video from her tiny Seoul studio on Sunday. By Monday there were two hundred comments.

Most were kind. One, from a user called Ingrid, said: "Glaze is running at the base every time. You're firing too hot." Three others called her talentless and worse.

Soo-ah felt her cheeks burn. For an hour she drafted replies to all of them, each nastier than the last. Then she deleted the drafts and looked again at her bowls. Ingrid was right about the glaze.

She replied only to Ingrid: "Thank you, I'll try a lower temperature on the next batch." She hid the insulting comments and didn't answer them.

The next week she posted the new bowls, glaze clean at the base. Ingrid commented: "Much better. Beautiful work." Soo-ah smiled and turned the laptop off.

qa.q: What did Ingrid say was causing the glaze to run?
qa.a: Ingrid said Soo-ah was firing too hot.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling when she drafted nasty replies?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt hurt and angry, with burning cheeks, after the insulting comments.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah separate useful criticism from abuse?
qa.a: She replied calmly to Ingrid's valid point about the glaze, hid the insults and didn't trade insults back.

qa.q: How might Ingrid have felt seeing the improved bowls?
qa.a: Ingrid likely felt pleased and respected, seeing that her critical comment was taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a young creator separating valid criticism from online abuse, replying calmly to one and not trading insults.

In the staff room of the Nashik public library, the new online review was on everyone's phone. "Staff are slow and the children's section is always messy. The young librarian, Lokesh, ignored me for ten minutes." It was signed Sarita K.

Below it, someone else had added: "Useless lazy people, shut it down."

Lokesh felt his throat tighten. He remembered the day: he'd been helping an elderly man with the catalogue.

"Reply and tell her she's lying," said a colleague.

Lokesh took a breath. "Part of it's fair. The children's section is messy."

He wrote: "Thank you, Sarita. We're sorry you waited. We're reorganising the children's section this month and adding a help bell at the desk." He didn't reply to the second comment.

Two weeks later, Sarita came back with her daughter and asked for Lokesh by name.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the library after reading Lokesh's reply?
qa.a: Sarita probably felt heard and respected, which is why she came back and asked for Lokesh by name.

Tenzin, playgroup
